fatal_errors: The proposed entropy-stabilization mechanism is opposite to the observed kinetically controlled behavior: diffusion becomes active, and Au/Cu surface segregation, melting, and evaporation destabilize the particles.
Adding elements does not isolate configurational entropy because it simultaneously changes mixing enthalpies, surface energies, atomic mobilities, melting behavior, and particle morphology.
The intervention omits the relevant controlled in situ vacuum-heating experiment on sub-10 nm equiatomic AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The predicted enhanced stability conflicts with the observed disappearance of small particles, shape evolution, broadened size distribution, and approximately 22% size reduction.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses high-temperature stability and gives a nominal baseline and falsification rule, but it reconstructs neither the material system nor the operative mechanism. The target evidence shows that high configurational entropy does not produce sluggish diffusion or preserve the initial structure: above roughly 673 K, surface-energy differences drive Au and Cu outward, with morphology-dependent diffusion followed by melting or evaporation near 973 K. The proposed high- versus low-element-count comparison is only moderately discriminating because composition is a major confounder. XRD may also miss surface segregation and local structural changes in sub-10 nm particles. A decisive test would instead track particle-resolved shape, size, Au/Cu surface enrichment, and elemental self-diffusivity during matched heating in vacuum, while controlling size, morphology, and composition-derived surface energies. No cited evidence supports the generated mechanism.
